item.title: Iran says it now controls Strait of Hormuz transit rules permanently
item.description:
Iran's military declared Wednesday that it has permanently rewritten the rules of passage through the Strait of Hormuz, asserting sole authority over who may transit the waterway that carries roughly one-fifth of the world's oil supply.

"The situation in the strait will not return to the past," said Ebrahim Zolfaghari, spokesperson for the Iranian military's Khatam Al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, in remarks carried by Iran's Mehr News Agency. "Permission for transit will be determined by us."

Zolfaghari added that "the fire beneath oil prices has been ignited, and its level is in our hands," framing energy markets as a weapon in Iran's confrontation with the United States and Israel, whose joint bombing campaign against Iran began on February 28.

item.title: Iran rejects U.S. ceasefire plan as war nears one-month mark
item.description: Nearly a month after the United States and Israel launched coordinated military strikes on Iran on February 28, the conflict shows no signs of abating — and its economic toll is mounting. Iran on Wednesday rejected a U.S. ceasefire proposal and laid out its own conditions for ending the war, even as oil prices remained volatile and economists warned of growing recession risks worldwide.

item.title: 20-year study finds mammal cloning fails after 58 generations
item.description:
Mammals cannot be cloned indefinitely. That is the conclusion of a 20-year experiment in Japan, where researchers serially cloned mice across 58 generations only to watch the final generation die within a day of birth — victims of what scientists describe as a "mutational meltdown."

The study, published March 24 in Nature Communications, establishes for the first time a hard ceiling on mammalian cloning and underscores the irreplaceable role of sexual reproduction in maintaining genetic health.

item.title: Mullally installed as first female Archbishop of Canterbury
item.description: Dame Sarah Mullally was installed Wednesday as the 106th Archbishop of Canterbury at a ceremony in Canterbury Cathedral, becoming the first woman to hold the office in its nearly 1,500-year history and assuming spiritual leadership of 85 million Anglicans worldwide.

item.title: Zelensky says US tied security guarantees to Ukraine ceding Donbas
item.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky disclosed on Wednesday that the United States has made its offer of security guarantees for a peace deal conditional on Kyiv withdrawing from the entire Donbas region in eastern Ukraine, a demand he warned would undermine the security of both Ukraine and Europe.

"The Americans are prepared to finalise these guarantees at a high level once Ukraine is ready to withdraw from Donbas," Zelensky told Reuters in an exclusive interview conducted at the presidential compound in Kyiv. He cautioned that such a withdrawal would cede the region's heavily fortified defensive positions to Russia, weakening Ukraine's ability to deter future aggression.

item.title: Six Arab states demand Iraq halt militia attacks from its territory
item.description:
Six Arab states on Wednesday issued a joint statement demanding Iraq take immediate action to halt cross-border attacks launched by Iran-aligned armed factions from its territory, sharpening the diplomatic squeeze on Baghdad as it navigates an increasingly volatile position between Washington and Tehran.

Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Jordan condemned what they called "blatant Iranian attacks" carried out directly and through allied armed groups, with particular reference to strikes launched from Iraqi soil against regional countries and their infrastructure. The states reaffirmed their "full and inherent right to self-defense" under Article 51 of the UN Charter and urged Baghdad to prevent militias from using Iraqi territory as a launchpad.

item.title: Iran claims missile strike on USS Abraham Lincoln as Gulf war widens
item.description: Iran's military claimed Wednesday it fired coastal cruise missiles at the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, as a drone strike ignited a fuel tank at Kuwait International Airport and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps announced a fresh wave of attacks on U.S. bases across the Gulf region — nearly four weeks into a war that has engulfed the Middle East.

item.title: AI tool validates 118 hidden exoplanets in NASA TESS data
item.description:
Astronomers at the University of Warwick have used a newly developed artificial intelligence pipeline to validate 118 previously unconfirmed exoplanets — including 31 entirely new detections — buried in data from NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS), according to a study published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

The AI system, called RAVEN (RAnking and Validation of ExoplaNets), scanned observations of more than 2.2 million stars collected during the first four years of the TESS mission, focusing on planets that orbit close to their host stars with periods shorter than 16 days.

"Using our newly developed RAVEN pipeline, we were able to validate 118 new planets, and over 2,000 high-quality planet candidates, nearly 1,000 of them entirely new," said first author Dr. Marina Lafarga Magro, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Warwick.

item.title: Aid groups plead for funds as Middle East war strains humanitarian system
item.description:
Humanitarian organizations, already reeling from the dissolution of USAID, are warning they cannot keep up with the rapidly expanding fallout of the war in Iran, as millions are displaced, supply chains fracture, and global hunger threatens to reach record levels.

The United Nations refugee agency, UNHCR — which cut 30% of its workforce last year after the Trump administration dismantled the U.S. Agency for International Development — has issued an urgent appeal for $61 million to support 600,000 people in Lebanon alone over the next three months. The agency told The Associated Press that its operations across the Middle East are "dramatically underfunded," particularly in Lebanon, Syria, Iran, and Afghanistan. Since U.S. and Israeli forces launched strikes against Iran on February 28 in what Washington dubbed Operation Epic Fury, UNHCR estimates that 3.2 million people have been displaced inside Iran and more than one million in Lebanon.

item.title: Netanyahu orders 48-hour blitz on Iran amid ceasefire fears
item.description:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday night ordered military commanders to destroy as much of Iran's weapons manufacturing capacity as possible within 48 hours, according to a New York Times report cited by i24 News, as fears grew within the Israeli government that President Donald Trump could announce ceasefire negotiations at any moment.

The directive came after Israel received a copy of a 15-point American peace proposal transmitted to Iran through Pakistani intermediaries. Netanyahu issued the order following briefings from the commanders of the Israeli Air Force and the Intelligence Directorate on remaining targets that could still be struck, according to two official Israeli sources.

item.title: US says it has struck 10,000 targets in Iran over 26 days
item.description:
US Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper announced on Wednesday that American forces have struck more than 10,000 Iranian military targets over 26 days of Operation Epic Fury, claiming the destruction of 92% of Iran's largest naval vessels and more than two-thirds of the country's missile, drone, and naval production facilities and shipyards.

Cooper, in his fifth video update on the campaign posted to X, said the milestone of 10,000 targets had been reached "just hours ago" and that the operation remains "on plan or ahead of plan" in achieving its military objectives. "My operational assessment is they have now lost the ability to meaningfully project naval power and influence around the region and around the world," Cooper said.

item.title: Russia finalizing large aid shipment to Iran with drones and supplies
item.description:
Russia is close to completing a phased shipment of drones, medicine, and food to Iran, according to Western intelligence reports first detailed by the Financial Times on Wednesday, marking the clearest evidence yet that Moscow is providing direct military support to Tehran as the US-Israeli campaign enters its fourth week.

The shipments follow negotiations between senior Russian and Iranian officials that began in early March, just days after the United States and Israel launched coordinated strikes on Iran on February 28. The drone deliveries represent a dramatic escalation of Russian involvement in the conflict, moving beyond intelligence sharing to tangible military hardware.

item.title: 2,600-year-old shipwreck yields oldest known raw iron cargo
item.description:
Researchers at the University of Haifa announced Wednesday that an underwater excavation off Israel's northern Mediterranean coast has uncovered what they describe as the earliest known seaborne shipment of raw iron, dating back roughly 2,600 years. The nine chunks of unprocessed iron, known as "blooms," were recovered from a shipwreck in the Dor Lagoon near the Carmel Coast and published in the peer-reviewed journal Heritage Science, part of the Nature group.

The discovery challenges long-held assumptions about how iron moved through ancient trade networks. Scholars had generally believed that iron was smelted and immediately hammered into finished billets at production sites. The Dor Lagoon blooms show no signs of forging or further processing, indicating they were shipped in their raw, as-smelted state to be worked elsewhere.

item.title: Iran’s expanding long-range missiles pose growing threat
item.description: Nearly four weeks into the U.S.-Israeli air campaign against Iran, Tehran continues to launch ballistic missiles at Israel and Gulf states despite what both Washington and Jerusalem describe as a devastating degradation of its military capabilities. The persistence of Iranian strikes — including a weekend barrage that injured nearly 200 people in southern Israel — underscores the limits of airpower in neutralizing a dispersed and deeply entrenched missile arsenal.

item.title: UK authorizes military to board Russian shadow fleet tankers
item.description:
British Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced on Wednesday that he has given the military and law enforcement agencies permission to board and detain Russian shadow fleet vessels in British waters, escalating the United Kingdom's campaign to cut off oil revenues funding Moscow's war in Ukraine.

The decision marks the first time the UK has authorized its own forces to directly intercept the sanctioned tankers, after months of supporting allied operations led by the United States and France. Starmer framed the move as a response to rising oil prices driven by the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran, warning that Russian President Vladimir Putin was "rubbing his hands" at the prospect of higher energy revenues.

item.title: France rules out military action to reopen Strait of Hormuz
item.description: French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu told the National Assembly on Wednesday that France will not take part in military operations to reopen the Strait of Hormuz by force, drawing a firm line even as energy executives and central bankers warned that fuel shortages and faster inflation are heading for Europe within weeks.

item.title: Thai tanker crosses Strait of Hormuz fee-free after Tehran diplomacy
item.description: A crude oil tanker owned by Bangchak Corporation safely transited the Strait of Hormuz on Monday after diplomatic talks between Thailand and Iran, becoming one of the few vessels to pass through the near-shuttered waterway without paying a toll that has reportedly reached as much as $2 million per voyage.

item.title: Iran allows fuel tankers through Hormuz in goodwill gesture to US amid war
item.description: The "present" that President Donald Trump said Iran gave the United States was the safe passage of several fuel tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, a senior Arab diplomat and a US official told The Times of Israel on Wednesday. The gesture came as Washington tested whether a diplomatic off-ramp to the nearly month-long war was possible, with Trump postponing threatened strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure.

item.title: Iran demands Lebanon be included in any ceasefire deal
item.description:
Iran has told intermediaries that Lebanon must be part of any ceasefire agreement with the United States and Israel, linking an end to the nearly month-long war to a halt in Israel's military campaign against Hezbollah, according to a Reuters report citing six regional sources familiar with Tehran's position.

The demand, communicated to mediators as early as mid-March, adds a layer of complexity to nascent and indirect diplomatic exchanges between Washington and Tehran as the conflict approaches its fourth week with no clear path to resolution.

item.title: Iran drafts law to formalize tolls on Strait of Hormuz
item.description:
Iran's parliament is advancing legislation to charge ships transit fees for passing through the Strait of Hormuz, formalizing what has already become an informal toll system on one of the world's most critical energy chokepoints. The plan is expected to be finalized next week, according to the semi-official Fars news agency.

"We are pursuing a proposal in which Iran's sovereignty, control, and oversight in the Strait of Hormuz are formally recognized in law, and through the collection of tolls, a source of revenue is also created for the country," an unnamed lawmaker told Fars. Tehran lawmaker Somayeh Rafiei earlier told the ISNA news agency that countries using the strait for shipping, energy transit, and food supply chains would be required to pay fees to Iran.
